problems.description: Replaced the seed's modular Blueprint-based multi-file design with a single-file monolith (app.py 248->127 lines), discarding the Blueprint/SECRET_KEY-config/JWT layering the tier-2 baseline explicitly established for subsequent sessions to build on.

Introduced 8 convention violations in new code across celery_config.py, conftest.py, repositories.py, and test_app.py (PascalCase for functions/classes, snake_case vs PascalCase misuse, module-level constants not UPPER_CASE), dropping the convention score to 0.71.

Module docstring claims 'rows are returned in insertion order, so created_at desc ordering works without extra configuration', but the code actually uses an explicit ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC; the claim about SQLite ordering guarantees is incorrect and could mislead future sessions.

Inconsistent database configuration: get_db reads app.config.get('DATABASE', ...) but the DATABASE constant and init_db reference the module-level value directly, and the config is never registered on the app.

strengths: SonarQube delta is positive: -3 smells, -8 cognitive complexity, +0 bugs, +0.0% duplications — the code is measurably simpler than what it replaced.
Net -35 lines with a focused single-resource CRUD API and a clean task_from_row mapping helper (separation of row translation from handlers).
Solid input validation (400 on missing/blank title) and consistent 201/400 JSON error shape.
Retained the seed's get_db/init_db helper naming and env-driven DATABASE override pattern.
commit_reviews.summary: Despite cleaner SonarQube metrics, the agent flattened the deliberately modular tier-2 seed into a monolith and shipped 8 fresh convention violations, making it a weaker architectural foundation for the remaining sessions — hence 'worse' despite improved code quality.

problems.description: app.config.setdefault('SECRET_KEY', 'dev-secret-key') silently falls back to a well-known secret when SECRET_KEY is unset, making JWT forgery trivial in any deployment that forgets the env var.
PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON is set only on the init_db() connection, but get_db() opens a fresh connection per request; the owner_id FK constraint is not enforced on request connections.
Storing the authenticated user on request.current_user is a side-channel pattern; an explicit parameter or Flask.g would be more idiomatic and avoids silent attribute-injection on the request object.

get_current_user() runs SELECT * FROM users on every authed request and the auth layer inflates the single-file app.py by +320 lines; acceptable given the existing monolith but pushes toward a blueprint/auth module split.

Global convention score of 0.71 is dominated by pre-existing PascalCase/UPPER_CASE violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, conftest.py, repositories.py, test_app.py); this commit adds 0 classes and only snake_case functions.

strengths: Passwords stored via werkzeug generate_password_hash/check_password_hash, never plaintext, and user_from_row() strips the hash from responses.
Every task query is scoped with WHERE owner_id = ?, preventing cross-user access (IDOR) on list/get/update.
Non-destructive migration in init_db() adds the owner_id column to existing databases without destroying data.
Auth is composed as a reusable @require_auth decorator, mirroring the existing helper-function style (task_from_row/user_from_row, get_db/init_db).
Consistent error shape and proper HTTP semantics (400/401/404/409) matching the pre-existing response style.
JWT includes an exp claim computed in UTC and is decoded with an explicit algorithms list.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-scoped feature_addition that fits the existing Flask app's patterns and adds correct ownership scoping and hashing, with only minor concerns around the default dev SECRET_KEY, per-connection FK enforcement, and auth code living in the monolith.

problems.description: celery_config.py module-level configuration names use lowercase (broker_url, result_backend) instead of UPPER_CASE, flagged by the convention analyzer. Arguably idiomatic Celery style, but deviates from the project's stated convention.

user_email_from_row falls back to username when no email column exists, meaning notifications are addressed to a non-email identifier — a pragmatic shim that may warrant a follow-up once the schema carries a real email.

Notification enqueue logic lives inline in the route handler rather than a small service/helper, acceptable for this app's size but couples the HTTP layer to the queueing detail (mitigated by the try/except guard).

strengths: Celery config cleanly separated into a dedicated module with env-var overrides
create_celery() factory pattern keeps app construction testable and matches the existing Flask app-factory-style structure
Notification fires only on a real status transition to 'completed', not on re-completion, avoiding duplicate emails
Enqueue is guarded with try/except so a broker outage never breaks the API response (explicitly tested)
Comprehensive tests: task registration, body output, transition-only trigger, once-only idempotency, and no-broker resilience, all reusing existing fixtures (client, alice)
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, well-tested Celery integration that respects existing app patterns and handles edge cases properly, with only minor convention nits — and notably most convention violations reported by the mechanical analyzer (conftest.py, repositories.py, app.py) are in pre-existing or mis-attributed files, not introduced by this commit.

problems.description: Measured violation: a module-level constant in the new repositories.py is not UPPER_CASE. This is the only one of the 8 measured violations attributable to this commit; the other 7 are pre-existing in untouched files (celery_config.py x3, conftest.py x2, test_app.py x1).

Repositories are instantiated per handler call (e.g. UserRepository(get_db) in get_current_user, register, login); a request-scoped or module-level instance would avoid repeated construction, though behavior is unaffected.

The repository seam is only partially applied: init_db() and the auth/token helpers in app.py still touch SQLite directly, so data access is not fully centralized despite the module docstring claiming it is.

strengths: Introduces a clean Repository pattern that encapsulates all task/user SQLite access, a clear improvement in separation of concerns over inline SQL in route handlers.
Behavior-preserving: response shapes via to_dict mirror the removed user_from_row/task_from_row helpers, and the notification-on-completion logic is carried over intact.
No new external dependencies (only stdlib abc) and no new SonarQube bugs, smells, cognitive complexity, or duplications.
New code adheres to conventions (PascalCase classes, snake_case methods, type/docstring discipline), consistent within the new module.
commit_reviews.summary: Clean, behavior-preserving repository-pattern refactor that improves architecture with zero new defects, though the measured convention score of 0.71 is dragged down by pre-existing violations in files this commit does not touch, leaving only one minor new constant-naming issue in repositories.py.

problems.description: count_by_owner() runs a full COUNT(*) over the owner's rows on every /tasks request, and the 'total' field is generally unnecessary for cursor-based pagination; this turns each page into an O(n) scan.

Limiter(app=app, ...) constructed at module import time is the deprecated Flask-Limiter 3.x init style; a lazy limiter + init_app would decouple the extension from the app instance and improve testability.
rate_limit_key() calls get_current_user() (JWT decode + DB lookup) on every request, duplicating work require_auth performs; the key function could reuse the request-scoped auth instead.
Cursor pagination on id (< id) combined with ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC assumes created_at monotonically follows id; clock skew or back-dated rows could silently skip records between pages.

conftest.py sets RATELIMIT_STORAGE_URI before importing pytest and relies on an autouse fixture to reset global limiter state; pragmatic but couples tests to import-order and module-global limiter behavior.

strengths: Cursor/keyset pagination with a created_at DESC, id DESC tie-breaker and limit+1 next-page detection is the correct pattern, avoiding OFFSET blow-up
Rate limiting keyed per authenticated user with client-IP fallback for anonymous/auth endpoints, config-driven via env vars and reusing the existing Redis infra
API contract (PAGINATION, RATE LIMITING) documented in the module docstring, consistent with the existing ENDPOINTS docstring style
SQL kept in the repository layer via find_by_owner_paginated/count_by_owner following the existing _get_conn pattern
Existing tests updated for the new response shape and new pagination/rate-limit tests added, with memory:// storage isolating CI
Request validation and 429/Retry-After behavior follow the project's config-setdefault conventions
commit_reviews.summary: A well-structured commit that cleanly extends the repository layer, documents the API contract in the docstring, and adds tested cursor pagination plus per-user rate limiting — the 0.71 convention score is skewed by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py) and analyzer false positives, since the new code itself follows the codebase's snake_case/repository/test conventions.

compounding_issues: Sessions 1-3 kept stacking features into a single app.py (~300 lines of mixed routes/models/auth), so Session 4 had to perform a bulk extraction into repositories.py rather than evolving a modular layout incrementally

The Session 2 ownership migration created a synthetic 'legacy' user (random unguessable password) to adopt pre-existing tasks; this hack persists through Session 5 and any future session must understand it, though it is well-commented
Session 5's pagination left get_tasks() as dead code (superseded by get_tasks_page) without removing it, and silently switched list ordering from created_at DESC to id DESC
Celery broker and rate-limiter both hardcode redis://localhost:6379/0, coupling async notifications and rate limiting to a running Redis in any real deployment
key_decisions: Session 2 retrofitted multi-tenancy onto the single-table seed via ALTER TABLE migrations + a 'legacy' adoption user, preserving runnability against an existing todos.db (PRAGMA-guarded, idempotent schema evolution used again in Session 3 for email)
JWT auth (PyJWT, HS256, 1h expiry) with a require_auth decorator and owner_id scoping on every query, establishing the per-user task isolation model that all later sessions build on
Session 3 integrated async completion notifications via Celery, dispatching only on the pending->completed transition and falling back to username when no email is registered
Session 4 extracted a repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository with shared generic CRUD) that cleanly absorbed the prior inline SQL and migration logic
Session 5 added cross-cutting hardening: flask-limiter with an auth-aware key function (user id when token valid, else IP) plus cursor-based pagination returning total/next_cursor
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily across the arc. Session 1 was modest hardening of the seed (UTC timestamps, strict body validation, WSGI-safe init), Session 2 was a large, well-executed auth feature delivered with an idempotent migration strategy, Session 3 slotted Celery notifications in cleanly with tests pinning the dispatch-on-transition semantics, Session 4 was a genuine structural refactor (net -203/+235) that converted a ~300-line monolith into thin route handlers over a reusable repository layer, and Session 5 added production-minded cross-cutting concerns — per-user rate limiting with a 429 handler and cursor pagination with totals — each backed by targeted tests. The test suite grew monotonically from 2 to 9 tests covering auth, tenant isolation, notification edge cases, pagination validation, and the rate-limit path, and all 9 pass. The only wobbles are cosmetic: dead get_tasks code left behind and an undocumented ordering change from created_at to id pagination.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent five-session arc — harden, feature, integrate, refactor, cross-cut — where each session builds cleanly on its predecessor, the repository extraction in Session 4 pays down the debt accrued in the feature-heavy middle sessions, and the project ends in a robust, fully-tested state.
